title: Foundations of Geometry
description: Points, lines, and planes; segment addition; midpoint and distance; angle pairs and angle addition; basic constructions.

practice.prompt: Point B is between A and C on a line. AB = 7 and BC = 12. Find AC.

figure.alt: Points A, B, and C on a line. AB is 7 and BC is 12. The whole length AC is unknown.

hints: Segment Addition Postulate: if B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC.
The two small pieces add up to the whole segment.

practice.prompt: M is the midpoint of segment AB. AM = 3x + 4 and MB = 5x − 6. Find the length of AB.

figure.alt: Segment AB with midpoint M. AM is 3x + 4 and MB is 5x − 6, marked congruent. AB is unknown.

hints: A midpoint cuts a segment into two equal pieces, so AM = MB.
Solve 3x + 4 = 5x − 6. You should get x = 5.
Plug x = 5 into AM, then double it (AB = AM + MB).

practice.prompt: Find the midpoint of the segment with endpoints (−2, 5) and (6, −1). Type it like (x, y).

figure.alt: A segment from (−2, 5) to (6, −1). Its midpoint is not shown.

hints: Midpoint formula: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Average the x's and average the y's.

practice.prompt: Find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (7, 10).

figure.alt: Points (1, 2) and (7, 10) joined by a segment, with a dashed run and rise under it.

hints: Distance formula: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). It's the Pythagorean theorem on the grid.

practice.prompt: Points A, B, and C are not on the same line (they are noncollinear). How many planes pass through all three points?

figure.alt: Three noncollinear points A, B, and C drawn on a slanted flat surface.

hints: A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
Think of a three-legged stool: it never wobbles, because three points fix one flat surface.
If the three points were on one line, a plane could spin around that line. Here they are not.
practice.solution: Through any three noncollinear points there is exactly one plane. (If they were collinear, there would be infinitely many.)

practice.prompt: ∠AOC and ∠COB are complementary. m∠AOC = 38°. Find m∠COB.

figure.alt: Angle AOB is split by ray OC. Angle AOC is 38 degrees and angle COB is marked x.

hints: Complementary angles add up to 90°.
Subtract 38 from 90.

practice.prompt: ∠ABD and ∠DBC form a linear pair. m∠ABD = (3x + 15)° and m∠DBC = (2x + 5)°. Find x.

figure.alt: Line AC with ray BD. Angle ABD is 3x + 15 degrees and angle DBC is 2x + 5 degrees.

hints: A linear pair sits on a straight line, so the two angles add to 180°.
Subtract 20, then divide by 5.

practice.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle measures (4x − 10)° and the angle vertical to it measures (2x + 30)°. Find x.

figure.alt: Two crossing lines. A pair of vertical angles is labeled 4x − 10 degrees and 2x + 30 degrees.

hints: Vertical angles are across from each other where two lines cross. They are congruent (equal).
Set them equal: 4x − 10 = 2x + 30.
Subtract 2x from both sides, then add 10.

practice.prompt: Point D is in the interior of ∠ABC. m∠ABD = 47° and m∠ABC = 112°. Find m∠DBC.

figure.alt: Angle ABC is 112 degrees with ray BD inside it. Angle ABD is 47 degrees and angle DBC is marked x.

hints: Angle Addition Postulate: m∠ABD + m∠DBC = m∠ABC.
Subtract 47 from 112.

practice.prompt: To construct the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, you draw an arc centered at A and an arc centered at B, then join the two points where the arcs cross (P and Q). What must be true about the compass width?

figure.alt: Segment AB with a circle drawn around A and a circle drawn around B. The circles cross at P and Q, and a dashed line joins P and Q.

choices: Keep the same width for both arcs, and make it more than half of AB
Use a width less than half of AB
Use one width at A and a different width at B
Set the width equal to exactly half of AB
practice.answer: Keep the same width for both arcs, and make it more than half of AB
hints: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A and from B.
If the widths were different, P and Q would not be equally far from A and B.
If the width were half of AB or less, would the arcs cross above and below the segment?
practice.solution: Use the same compass width from A and from B, more than half of AB. Then P and Q are each equally far from A and B, and line PQ is the perpendicular bisector. Too small a width and the arcs never meet.

flashcards.back: Point: a location (no size). Line: straight, goes on forever both ways. Plane: a flat surface that goes on forever. These are the undefined terms of geometry.
Collinear: on the same line. Coplanar: on the same plane. Any 3 noncollinear points lie on exactly one plane.
If B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC.

figure.alt: Points A, B, C on a line; AB plus BC equals AC.

flashcards.back: The point that splits a segment into two congruent halves. If M is the midpoint of AB, then AM = MB = ½ AB.
M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Average the x's, average the y's.
d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). It is the Pythagorean theorem on a coordinate grid.
Two angles whose measures add to 90°. Example: 38° and 52°.
Two angles whose measures add to 180°. Example: 127° and 53°.
The angles across from each other when two lines cross. Vertical angles are congruent.

figure.alt: Two crossing lines with vertical angles 1 and 2 across from each other.

flashcards.back: Two adjacent angles whose outer sides make a straight line. They are supplementary (add to 180°).

figure.alt: Line AC with ray BD making adjacent angles 1 and 2 that together form a straight angle.

flashcards.back: If D is in the interior of ∠ABC, then m∠ABD + m∠DBC = m∠ABC. An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal angles.
Copy a segment, copy an angle, bisect an angle, and construct a perpendicular bisector. Keep the compass width the same when the steps say so.

figure.alt: Points A, B, C on a line. AB is 2x + 3, BC is 4x − 1, and AC is 32.

quiz.prompt: Two angles are supplementary. One measures 127°. Find the other.

figure.alt: Two angles that form a straight line. One is 127 degrees and the other is marked x.

hints: Supplementary angles add to 180°.

quiz.prompt: Find the midpoint of the segment with endpoints (4, −3) and (−8, 7). Type it like (x, y).

figure.alt: A segment from (4, −3) to (−8, 7). Its midpoint is not shown.

hints: Average the x's and average the y's.

figure.alt: Points (−1, −2) and (4, 10) joined by a segment.

hints: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).

quiz.prompt: Two lines cross and one of the four angles is 64°. What are the other three angles?

figure.alt: Two crossing lines. One of the four angles is 64 degrees.

hints: The angle across from 64° is its vertical angle.
The angles next to 64° form linear pairs with it (add to 180°).

quiz.prompt: Ray QS bisects ∠PQR. m∠PQS = 34°. Find m∠PQR.

figure.alt: Angle PQR split by ray QS into two equal angles. Angle PQS is 34 degrees.

hints: A bisector splits the angle into two equal halves.
The whole angle is twice one half.
